channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: Comparative Efficacy and Acceptability of Transdiagnostic Psychotherapies for Emotional Disorders: Protocol for a Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Emotional disorders (anxiety and unipolar depression) are common and disabling, and disorder-specific CBT (DS-CBT) is a gold standard but may be inefficient with comorbidity and service constraints. This is a protocol for a network meta-analysis (NMA) comparing transdiagnostic psychotherapies (e.g., Unified Protocol, transdiagnostic behavior therapy), DS-CBT, other evidence-based therapies (e.g., ACT, behavioral activation), and control conditions in adults with anxiety and/or depressive disorders.
FINDINGS: The NMA will include RCTs from major databases (PubMed, Embase, PsycInfo, Cochrane Library) and existing meta-analytic databases. Eligible participants are adults (≥18 years) with a principal diagnosis of anxiety and/or unipolar depressive disorder or scoring above validated cutoffs on anxiety/depression scales. Primary outcomes are continuous measures of anxiety and depressive symptom severity at posttreatment; secondary outcomes include study dropout (acceptability) and response/remission where available. The analysis will use random-effects NMA within a frequentist framework (netmeta package in R) and Bayesian NMA as sensitivity analyses. As of September 2026, literature search is complete, title/abstract screening is ongoing, and data analysis is planned for late 2026, with results expected in early 2027.
INTERPRETATION: This is a protocol for an NMA, so no results are available yet. The planned methodology appears robust (random-effects NMA, frequentist and Bayesian approaches, examination of transitivity and consistency), but the findings are pending. The study aims to provide a comprehensive comparative evaluation, which could inform clinical decision-making and guideline development if the results are robust and clinically meaningful.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No clinical implications can be drawn yet, as the study is still in progress. Once published, the results may help clinicians choose between transdiagnostic psychotherapies, DS-CBT, and other evidence-based treatments based on efficacy and acceptability rankings.

item.title: Effectiveness of Virtual Reality Versus Exercise-Based Interventions in the Management of Chronic Spinal Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared virtual reality (VR) with exercise-based interventions for adults with chronic spinal pain, focusing on pain, disability, fear of movement, and quality of life. Fifteen RCTs (n=659) were included, with most judged at high risk of bias.
FINDINGS: Very low-certainty evidence showed statistically significant but small reductions in pain (VAS: MD −1.05, 95% CI −1.92 to −0.18; p=0.02; NPRS: MD −0.95, 95% CI −1.59 to −0.31; p=0.003) and kinesiophobia (MD −3.52, 95% CI −6.08 to −0.96; p=0.007) favouring VR. No significant difference was found for disability (MD −1.38, 95% CI −5.43 to 2.67; p=0.50), and quality-of-life results were heterogeneous.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is very low certainty due to high risk of bias, substantial heterogeneity (I² up to 94%), and failure to reach MCID thresholds. While p-values suggest statistical superiority for pain and fear of movement, the clinical relevance is uncertain. Larger, well-designed RCTs with active comparators and patient-centred outcomes are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify routine use of VR over exercise-based therapy for chronic spinal pain; clinicians should await higher-quality trials before changing practice.

item.title: Exercise to enhance antipsychotic effectiveness and mitigate metabolic harm: systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO registered) evaluated whether supervised exercise interventions improve psychiatric outcomes and mitigate antipsychotic-induced metabolic harm in adults with schizophrenia or related psychotic disorders. Twenty-eight RCTs (n = 1119) published since 2000 were included.
FINDINGS: Exercise significantly improved negative symptoms (MD −3.08, 95% CI −4.46 to −1.70; p < 0.001), general psychopathology (−2.18, −4.14 to −0.22; p = 0.034), and PANSS total score (−7.07, −13.29 to −0.85; p = 0.030). Positive symptoms were not significantly affected (−1.22, −2.46 to 0.02; p = 0.053). Metabolic benefits included reduced body weight (−1.62 kg, −3.08 to −0.16; p = 0.034), body fat percentage (−1.25%, −2.17 to −0.33; p = 0.020), and waist circumference (−1.42 cm, −2.65 to −0.20; p = 0.032). No significant effects were found for BMI, blood pressure, fasting glucose, or most lipid measures. GRADE certainty was moderate for negative symptoms and metabolic outcomes, low to very low for others.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests supervised exercise can modestly improve core psychopathology and reduce adiposity in people on antipsychotics, with moderate-quality evidence for key outcomes. However, effect sizes are small (e.g., ~3-point PANSS reduction), and metabolic benefits did not extend to clinically critical endpoints like glucose or lipids. Heterogeneity in exercise types, small sample sizes, and short follow-ups limit conclusions. High-quality RCTs with standardized multicomponent exercise and comprehensive metabolic monitoring are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Supervised exercise may serve as a useful adjunct to antipsychotic treatment, particularly for negative symptoms and weight management, but current evidence does not support major changes in metabolic risk management. Clinicians should consider integrating supervised exercise as part of holistic care while monitoring for modest benefits.

item.title: Perceived Utility of Combining Atypical Long-Acting Injectable Antipsychotics With Psychosocial Interventions: An Exploratory Survey of Mid-Career Psychiatrists in Japan.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study explored mid-career Japanese psychiatrists' attitudes toward combining atypical long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAIs) with psychosocial interventions for schizophrenia, using an anonymous cross-sectional web-based survey (n=69 complete responses out of 1038 invited).
FINDINGS: Psychiatrists with a positive attitude toward LAIs were significantly more likely to perceive the combination as useful for psychosocial treatment (p=0.038), financial/employment support (p=0.015), and housing support (p=0.041), but not for day/night care (p=0.090) or community care (p=0.079). The most cited rationales for the combination were improved adherence, relapse prevention, and synergistic effects.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary due to a very low response rate (6.6%), small sample size, and selection bias (predominantly male, self-selected participants). The associations reported are statistically significant but based on exploratory analyses without adjustment for multiple comparisons. The generalizability to broader psychiatric practice is limited, and the clinical significance of these perceptions remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study does not provide actionable evidence to change practice but suggests a perceived benefit of combining LAIs with psychosocial support among a subset of Japanese psychiatrists. Further research with larger, representative samples is needed to validate these findings.

item.title: Australian Digital Mental Health Services for Anxiety and Depression: Meta-Analysis and Comparison Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This meta-analysis and comparison study evaluated the uptake and effectiveness of three Australian government-funded digital mental health services (DMHSs: Mental Health Online, MindSpot, THIS WAY UP) for adults with anxiety and depression, comparing their outcomes to other mental health treatments using routinely collected service data (2013–2021) and published literature.
FINDINGS: The three DMHSs served over 282,000 consumers. Clinician-supported treatments showed large pooled effect sizes (Cohen d: Mental Health Online 0.95, MindSpot 1.42, THIS WAY UP 1.04), while self-directed treatment by Mental Health Online showed a moderate effect (Cohen d=0.59). Clinician-supported DMHS outcomes were comparable to face-to-face, phone, and stepped-care comparators, though heterogeneity across services and clinical need levels was noted.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests DMHSs deliver clinically meaningful improvements in anxiety and depression symptoms, particularly with clinician support. However, heterogeneity in effect sizes and comparator populations limits firm conclusions about equivalence across settings. The reliance on aggregated service data and varied literature sources introduces potential bias, and no direct randomized comparisons were made. Further high-quality trials are needed to confirm effectiveness across diverse populations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: DMHSs may offer accessible, effective alternatives to traditional care for mild-to-moderate anxiety and depression, especially where clinician support is available. Clinicians should consider these services for patients preferring digital interventions, while monitoring for variability in outcomes and ensuring appropriate clinical oversight.

item.title: Randomised controlled trial of fluoxetine versus naltrexone in compulsive sexual behaviour disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study is an open-label RCT comparing fluoxetine and naltrexone for compulsive sexual behaviour disorder (CSBD) in 80 adults (79 men, 1 woman) over 8 weeks of treatment followed by 6 weeks without treatment, assessing symptom reduction using the HD:CAS scale.
FINDINGS: No statistically significant difference in HD:CAS score reduction was found between fluoxetine (n=40) and naltrexone (n=40) at the primary endpoint (week 8). Adverse events led to discontinuation in 5.1% (fluoxetine) and 15% (naltrexone) of participants, with additional non-serious discontinuations in both groups (10.3% fluoxetine, 15% naltrexone). Symptom trajectories differed between treatments over time.
INTERPRETATION: The open-label design and lack of blinding risk bias in subjective symptom ratings, and the small sample size limits power to detect small but potentially meaningful differences. The differing adverse effect profiles and symptom trajectories suggest potential individualised treatment considerations, but the absence of a statistically significant primary outcome means conclusions about superiority are unsupported. Further blinded, larger trials are needed to clarify comparative efficacy and tolerability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support choosing naltrexone over fluoxetine for CSBD based on efficacy; treatment choice may instead be guided by adverse effect profiles and patient preference until higher-quality evidence emerges.

item.title: A longitudinal analysis of the clinical practice of ketamine assisted psychotherapy with adolescents and young adults.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Ketamine-assisted psychotherapy (KAP) is being explored for adolescents and young adults with severe, treatment-resistant mental health conditions in a community outpatient setting. This longitudinal case series examines feasibility, tolerability, and symptom change over repeated sessions in 19 patients aged 14–24 years.
FINDINGS: In 19 adolescents/young adults (mean age 19.3 ± 3.1 years; 11 female, 7 male, 1 non-binary) completing ≥3 KAP sessions, BDI-II scores decreased by an estimated 0.65 points per visit (95% CI: -0.90, -0.40) and HAM-A scores by 0.21 points per visit (95% CI: -0.44, +0.01) in linear mixed-effects models. Individual treatment effects were medium/large in 63.2% (12/19) on BDI and 47.4% (9/19) on HAM-A. Overall benefit was reported in 68.4% (13/19) of cases, with reductions in suicidality. Ketamine was well tolerated across 167 sessions; nausea occurred in 5.4% and was manageable. No hospitalizations, misuse, or neurological harm were observed over a median follow-up of 5.6 months (mean 10.1, range 0.9–36.4).
INTERPRETATION: This uncontrolled, single-site case series suggests potential symptomatic benefit and good tolerability of KAP in a diagnostically complex adolescent population. However, the absence of a control group, small sample, and reliance on clinician/patient-reported outcomes limit causal inference. The observed per-visit symptom reductions are statistically significant but modest in magnitude, and their clinical significance remains uncertain without comparator data. Larger, randomized trials with longer follow-up are needed to confirm efficacy, safety, and durability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine use of KAP in adolescents outside research or highly specialized settings. Clinicians should remain cautious, monitor closely for adverse effects, and consider this modality only within structured protocols with informed consent and safeguards.

item.title: Patients' experiences of and adherence to supervised high-intensity physical training integrated into specialised treatment for substance use disorders: study protocol for a qualitative collaborative health services study of facilitators and barriers.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Persons with substance use disorders (SUDs) have elevated risks of lifestyle-related diseases and reduced life expectancy. This qualitative collaborative health services study protocol examines inpatients' experiences of and adherence to supervised high-intensity physical training (HIT) integrated into specialised SUD treatment, aiming to identify facilitators and barriers to adherence.
FINDINGS: The study will purposively recruit ~20 inpatients with SUDs (10 adherent and 10 non-adherent to HIT) for in-depth semi-structured interviews. Data collection includes interviews, reflexive field notes, and collaborative thematic analysis with persons with lived experience. The protocol does not report preliminary findings.
INTERPRETATION: As a qualitative protocol, no results are available to evaluate. The study design prioritises depth and patient-centred insights but may be limited by small, purposive sampling and reliance on self-reported adherence. Findings will depend on the rigor of thematic analysis and the representativeness of the sample. The collaborative approach with lived experience is a strength but may introduce bias. Results are preliminary and will require validation in larger, quantitative studies.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study may inform person-centred strategies to improve adherence to HIT in SUD treatment, but no clinical recommendations can be made until results are available. Clinicians should await empirical findings before considering changes to practice.

item.title: Risk-Stratified Cardiac Monitoring During Antipsychotic Treatment in Adolescents and Young Adults.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This structured narrative review aimed to develop a risk-stratified framework for cardiac monitoring (ECG and electrolytes) in adolescents and young adults receiving antipsychotics, focusing on QTc prolongation and sudden cardiac death risk. The review prioritized youth-specific evidence but incorporated adult data where necessary, synthesizing findings narratively without formal risk-of-bias assessment.
FINDINGS: Patient-level factors (e.g., electrolyte disturbances, bradycardia, restrictive eating disorders, thyroid dysfunction, inherited channelopathies, structural heart disease, and interacting drugs) were more consistently linked to QTc risk than specific antipsychotics. Ziprasidone and pimozide showed the strongest drug-related signals in youth, while sertindole, iloperidone, high-dose phenothiazines, and amisulpride (in overdose or renal impairment) posed risks in adults. Clozapine required separate myocarditis surveillance. The framework recommends tiered baseline risk assessment with targeted ECG/electrolyte monitoring, repeat testing driven by risk factors, treatment changes, or agent-specific warnings.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is broad but heterogeneous, with narrative synthesis and no formal risk-of-bias or certainty assessment, limiting confidence in the conclusions. The review’s strength lies in its comprehensive search and prioritization of youth-specific data, but the lack of quantitative synthesis and prospective validation of the proposed framework weakens internal validity. The clinical recommendations are plausible but remain untested, and the identified risk factors should guide monitoring until prospective studies validate the tiered approach.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The proposed risk-stratified monitoring framework may refine current practice by emphasizing targeted rather than uniform ECG/electrolyte testing in young antipsychotic users, particularly those with identified vulnerabilities. Clinicians should prioritize high-risk patients (e.g., those with electrolyte imbalances or restrictive eating disorders) and exercise caution with ziprasidone, pimozide, and clozapine, but prospective validation is needed before definitive practice changes.

item.title: Adverse childhood experiences and risk of chronic sleep disturbances: A population-based cohort study from a Chinese national survey.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This population-based cohort study from China examined whether adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) increase the risk of chronic sleep disturbances in older adults, using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). The study aimed to quantify the association between ACEs and sleep disturbances in a large sample of adults aged ≥45 years, excluding those with psychiatric conditions.
FINDINGS: Among 5,533 participants, the adjusted odds ratio (OR) for chronic sleep disturbances increased with ACE exposure: OR 1.30 (95% CI: 1.05–1.59) for 1 ACE, OR 1.60 (1.28–1.99) for 2 ACEs, and OR 2.10 (1.69–2.62) for ≥3 ACEs (Ptrend < 0.001). Household mental illness showed the strongest association (OR = 1.77, 1.53–2.06, P < 0.001). Subgroup analyses across most strata showed elevated risks (OR range: 1.27–1.81, P < 0.05).
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates a dose–response relationship between ACEs and chronic sleep disturbances in older Chinese adults, with a twofold increased risk in those with ≥3 ACEs. The large sample size and consistent subgroup findings strengthen internal validity, though residual confounding (e.g., unmeasured psychiatric or socioeconomic factors) and reliance on self-reported sleep data limit causal inference. The effect size, while statistically significant, reflects prevalence differences rather than clinical severity; whether targeted interventions would reduce sleep disturbances remains untested.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider screening older adults with significant ACE histories for sleep disturbances, particularly those exposed to household mental illness. However, routine ACE screening solely for sleep risk is premature without evidence that interventions mitigate outcomes.

item.title: Associations between perceived stress, sleep quality, and suicidal ideation among Chinese graduating-grade secondary school students: a multi-method study of the moderating role of physical exercise.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study examined whether perceived stress and sleep quality are linked to suicidal ideation in 4,372 Chinese high-school students (grades 9 and 12), and whether physical exercise weakens these associations. The authors also used machine-learning and network analysis to identify key predictors of suicidal ideation.
FINDINGS: Perceived stress was positively associated with suicidal ideation (β not reported; mediation model adjusted for demographics). Sleep quality partially mediated this link (indirect effect β ≈ 0.08, 95 % CI 0.06–0.10). Physical exercise moderated both the direct stress–suicide link and the sleep–suicide link: higher exercise levels attenuated these relationships (interaction p < 0.01). Machine-learning models (ridge regression and gradient boosting) predicted suicidal ideation with R² ≈ 0.41 in hold-out testing; SHAP values ranked sleep problems, stress, exercise, and their interactions among the top predictors. Network analysis highlighted subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep disturbances, stress-coping burden, and exercise frequency as central nodes.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests perceived stress and poor sleep are risk factors for suicidal ideation in this adolescent population, and that physical exercise may buffer these risks. However, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the mediation/moderation effects are small (indirect β ≈ 0.08). Machine-learning performance (R² ≈ 0.41) indicates moderate predictive power but does not establish clinical utility. Funding sources and potential unmeasured confounders (e.g., family history, prior mental health care) are not reported, limiting internal validity. External validity may be constrained by the specific regional sample and self-report measures.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Findings support incorporating stress-reduction, sleep-improvement, and exercise-promotion components into school mental-health programs, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend exercise as a standalone suicide-prevention strategy. Clinicians should assess sleep and stress in at-risk students while awaiting longitudinal or interventional confirmation.

item.title: A data-driven methodological framework for representative recruitment in psychiatric research: insights from the DOCUMENT study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Slow participant recruitment is one of the predominant determinants of failure or delay across clinical research. Even when recruitment targets are met, study populations may be unrepresentative due to sampling biases introduced by recruitment pathways. However, the effectiveness and demographic consequences of recruitment strategies are frequently underreported, undermining the generalisability of clinical findings and contributing to research waste.

item.title: Reliability of Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition, Assessments Using Telepsychiatry for Children With Neurodevelopmental Disorders and Their Caregivers: Randomized Feasibility Study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: The COVID-19 pandemic has increased the demand for telepsychiatry in neurodevelopmental assessment; however, few studies have examined the interrater reliability of clinician-rated autism scales, such as the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition (CARS2), when used remotely. Although the feasibility and validity of telehealth assessments have been explored previously, the consistency between remote and in person CARS2 ratings by different clinicians remains underinvestigated.

item.title: Ask autistic adolescents too: informant discrepancies and test-retest reliability in social behavior.
item.description: Assumptions about autistic youths' inability to accurately self-report their own behavior have limited what is known about adolescent-parent informant discrepancies. Across two randomized controlled trials, autistic adolescents (10-18 years) and their parents independently reported on adolescents' social skills and problem behaviors approximately 2-3 months apart. Test-retest reliability was evaluated among control-condition dyads (N = 40). Adolescent reports demonstrated moderate test-retest reliability across both domains. There were no group differences in reporting of social skills.

item.title: Accelerated brain aging as a transdiagnostic biomarker: A lifespan MRI brain age study across seven disorders.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Accelerated brain aging has been associated with several neuropsychiatric disorders; however, findings remain inconsistent due to limited lifespan modeling and inadequate age-bias correction. This study aimed to establish normative brain-aging trajectories across the lifespan and quantify disorder-specific deviations in brain-predicted age difference (brain-PAD) in a large, age-diverse sample.

item.title: Molecular mechanisms of electroconvulsive therapy modulates excitation-inhibition balance in major depression disorder.
item.description: BACKGROUND: The excitation-inhibition (E/I) imbalance is a major pathological characteristic of major depressive disorder (MDD). However, whether/how electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) modulates neuronal homeostasis or E/I balance in MDD and its molecular basis is still largely unknown. METHODS: In this study, longitudinal rs-fMRI data from 46 patients with MDD receiving ECT and 46 healthy controls were included.

item.title: Executive functions as a transdiagnostic endophenotype in developmental psychopathology.
item.description: The majority of mental health conditions emerges before adulthood, with prevalence increasing especially during childhood and adolescence. Coupled with high comorbidity between disorders, there is an urgent need to identify transdiagnostic mechanisms that underpin both risk and resilience to developmental psychopathology. Here we propose executive functions (EFs), a set of cognitive processes relevant for goal-directed control of thought and actions, as a promising candidate for such a mechanism.

item.title: Acetaminophen produces limited molecular and functional effects in human cortical organoids.
item.description: Acetaminophen (APAP) is the most widely used analgesic during pregnancy, yet its effects on prenatal human brain development remain incompletely understood. Epidemiological studies have reported inconsistent associations between prenatal APAP exposure and later neurodevelopmental outcomes, underscoring the need for mechanistic evaluation in human-relevant developmental models. Here, we examined how APAP influences early cortical development using induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cortical organoids (COs) generated from six independent lines.

item.title: Association between polygenic liability to depression and lifetime depression in at-risk adolescents.
item.description: Internalising symptoms including depression, anxiety and somatic symptoms in adolescence are common. They can be transient, but they can also persist and progress to major depressive disorder (MDD) Polygenic risk scores for major depression (MD-PGS) may help identify which symptomatic adolescents are at greatest risk of later disorder. In a mega-analysis of two longitudinal population-based cohorts from Brisbane, Australia, we investigated whether polygenic liability to depression improves risk stratification among adolescents with elevated internalising symptoms.

item.title: Six-year clinical course of depressive and anxiety disorders: analysis by age.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Evidence on the association between age and the long-term course of affective disorders remains mixed. OBJECTIVE: This study examined the 6-year symptom and diagnostic trajectories of depression and anxiety in relation to age, and assessed whether social, lifestyle, somatic and clinical factors explained observed age-related differences. METHODS: A cohort of 1701 participants aged 18-65 years with a current depressive and/or anxiety disorder from the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety were assessed biennially over 6 years.

item.title: Patient Perspectives on Offers of Buprenorphine in the Emergency Department.
item.description: IMPORTANCE: Buprenorphine reduces mortality in opioid use disorder (OUD), and emergency department-initiated buprenorphine (EDIB) doubles 30-day treatment retention, yet many patients decline EDIB when offered. Patient-driven factors limiting uptake are not well characterized. OBJECTIVE: To identify factors associated with patients accepting or declining EDIB.

item.title: Parkinson's disease-associated psychosis in a Brazilian sample: prevalence and clinical profile.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Psychosis is a frequent and disabling non-motor complication of Parkinson's disease (PD). Reported prevalence varies widely, and data in Brazilian cohorts remain scarce. OBJECTIVE: To estimate the prevalence of PD-associated psychosis (PDP) in a Brazilian cohort and to describe its sociodemographic and clinical profile. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study in a Brazilian movement disorders outpatient clinic between May and December of 2022.

item.title: Paediatric-Pharmacy Shared Care Improves Access and Efficiency in Developmental Paediatrics.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Rising prevalence of neurodevelopmental disorders, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), has increased demand for developmental paediatric services. Ongoing medication review requirements place increasing pressure on paediatrician-led models. Pharmacist-led shared care may improve capacity and access; however, evidence in paediatric outpatient settings remains limited. AIM: To evaluate the impact of a paediatric-pharmacy shared-care model on wait times, service capacity and efficiency compared with medical-only care.

item.title: Patient Travel Experiences for Methadone Dosing Visits.
item.description: IMPORTANCE: Patients often experience travel-related barriers to methadone dosing at opioid treatment programs (OTPs), but the nature of their experiences are not well understood. OBJECTIVE: To characterize patient experiences with travel to OTPs for regular methadone dosing visits at a large multisite OTP in Washington state. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This qualitative study utilized an embedded mixed-methods design.

item.title: Unlocking the Power of Neighborhood Collective Efficacy: Associations with ADHD and Youth Outcomes Among Black and White Adolescents.
item.description: This study examined the associations of neighborhood collective efficacy and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) status with psychosocial and academic outcomes among Black and White adolescents. Using a sample of 2,178 adolescents (ages 14-19; 73.0% Black, 27.0% White) from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study, we investigated how adolescent- and caregiver-reported neighborhood collective efficacy, and its interactions with racial group and ADHD status, were associated with wellbeing and school-related outcomes.

item.title: Estimating direct and indirect genetic effects on emerging variation in depressive symptoms in early adolescence: a trio polygenic score analysis in the MoBa cohort : Author list.
item.description: Early adolescence is a common period of onset for depressive symptoms. In part, this may reflect a developmental expression of individuals' genetic propensities as they undergo physiological and hormonal changes and interact with new environments. Many commonly proposed mechanisms assume direct effects of an individual's own genes on emerging variation in their depressive symptomatology. However, estimates of genetic influence based on analyses in unrelated individuals capture not only direct genetic effects but also genetic effects from parents and other biologically related family members.

item.title: Improvement in Domestic Violence and Aggression in Comorbid ADHD and Conduct Disorder Following Methylphenidate Initiation: A Case Report.
item.description: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and conduct disorder (CD) are diagnoses that are frequently comorbid. CD is characterised by persistent dissocial, aggressive, and defiant behaviors that defy age-appropriate expectations. This is the case of a 15-year-old male adoptee referred to Tier 3 Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS) for severe aggression, impulsivity, and domestic violence.

item.title: Daily-Level Drinking Motives as Predictors of Transdermal Alcohol Concentration and Alcohol-Induced Blackouts Among Young Adults.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Alcohol use is necessary-but not sufficient-for understanding why individuals experience an alcohol-induced blackout (AIB). Drinking motives are one of the most proximal risk factors for alcohol use. This study conducts a comprehensive within-person examination of AIBs predicted by prospective daily reports of drinking motives and alcohol use measured using a transdermal alcohol concentration (TAC) biosensor.

item.title: Family Medicine at the Forefront: Advancing Telemedicine for Opioid Use Disorder (TeleOUD) Through Access, Trust, and Community-Centered Care.
item.description: Telemedicine for opioid use disorder (teleOUD) represents a critical opportunity to expand access to evidence-based treatment while reducing stigma and structural barriers that have long impeded recovery. Yet, gaps persist in awareness, education, and trust among both clinicians and patients. Family medicine, grounded in continuity, collaboration, and community-centered care, is uniquely positioned to close these gaps.

item.title: Linked multimodal brain alterations in depression with suicidal risk.
item.description: Suicidal ideation and behavior (SIB) represent a major clinical challenge in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the multimodal brain structural signatures associated with SIB and their relationships with cognitive dysfunction remain poorly understood. We acquired multimodal neuroimaging measures, including gray matter volume, cortical thickness, pial area (PA), white matter fractional anisotropy, together with neurocognitive measures from 61 MDD patients with SIB (MDD-SIB), 38 without SIB (MDD-nSIB), and 142 healthy controls (HC).

item.title: Improved Social Functioning Mediated the Effects of Adolescents' Sports Participation on Self-Harm and Psychological Wellbeing: A Prospective Cohort Study.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: The prevalence of self-harm, regardless of the presence of suicidal intent or not, has been increasing, and effective and accessible intervention strategies are needed. This study investigated whether sports participation in adolescence serves as a protective factor against the future development of self-harm or poor psychological wellbeing, as well as the relevant psychosocial mechanisms.

item.title: Nutraceuticals and phytoceuticals in the treatment of bipolar disorder: A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and network meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and acceptability of nutraceuticals and phytoceuticals (e.g., vitamins, herbal products) for treating bipolar disorder (BD) in randomized controlled trials (RCTs), addressing a gap in evidence for these adjunctive or alternative treatments.
FINDINGS: Twenty-eight RCTs (n=2,222) assessed 22 treatments. No nutraceutical outperformed placebo for depressive symptoms; placebo outperformed palmitoylethanolamide (SMD=2.69, 95% CI 1.43–3.95) in one trial with high heterogeneity (I²=86%). For manic symptoms, palmitoylethanolamide (SMD=-4.58, 95% CI -6.24 to -2.92) and folic acid (SMD=-2.42, 95% CI -4.06 to -0.79) outperformed placebo, but with substantial heterogeneity (I²=91.3%). Only one RCT supported palmitoylethanolamide’s effect, and meta-regression linked larger effects to lower methodological quality (AMSTAR-Plus scores). Confidence in evidence (CINeMA) was predominantly low or very low.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak, with high heterogeneity, reliance on single small trials, and low methodological quality ratings. The statistically significant findings for manic symptoms are not robust due to inconsistency, small sample sizes, and potential bias. No treatment can be recommended based on current data; further high-quality RCTs are urgently needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should not use nutraceuticals or phytoceuticals as evidence-based treatments for acute bipolar depression or mania. Patients using these products should be monitored closely, and clinicians should discuss the lack of robust evidence supporting their efficacy.

item.title: Pharmacological interventions for alcohol use disorder on quality of life: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 randomized controlled trials (n=4376) examined whether pharmacotherapies for alcohol use disorder (AUD) improve mental and physical quality of life (QoL), a key outcome for sustaining recovery.
FINDINGS: Naltrexone improved both mental QoL (d=0.30, 95% CI 0.08–0.52) and physical QoL (d=0.16, 95% CI 0.01–0.31). Nalmefene improved physical QoL (d=0.13, 95% CI 0.02–0.25) but not mental QoL (d=0.18, 95% CI –0.004 to 0.354). Topiramate showed no clear benefit, though a post-hoc analysis suggested a small physical QoL gain linked to reduced heavy drinking. Evidence for other agents (acamprosate, sertraline, psilocybin) was based on single trials.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate in size but heterogeneous, with small effect sizes and limited data for many drugs. Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane RoB 2, but selective reporting and heterogeneity limit certainty. Statistically significant effects do not necessarily translate into clinically meaningful improvements in daily functioning or well-being.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current pharmacotherapies may offer modest QoL benefits for some patients with AUD, but routine QoL monitoring is not yet supported by robust evidence. Clinicians should individualize treatment and consider QoL outcomes alongside traditional measures like abstinence or relapse rates.

item.title: Psychosocial interventions for military personnel with PTSD: protocol of a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks which psychosocial interventions are most effective for military personnel with PTSD and how their components compare, using a planned network meta-analysis of existing trials. This matters because PTSD is common in this population and multiple therapies exist but head-to-head evidence is sparse.
FINDINGS: The protocol describes a systematic review followed by network meta-analysis to compare all psychological interventions for PTSD in current and former military personnel. It will also examine which specific treatment components drive benefit when delivered in combination. The team will involve lived-experience advisors, clinicians and researchers throughout.
INTERPRETATION: Because this is a protocol rather than completed analyses, no effect sizes, confidence intervals or p-values are yet available. The planned methods (network meta-analysis) can rank treatments even when they have never been directly compared, but the eventual certainty of the evidence will depend on the number and quality of included studies, their comparators and risk of bias. Involvement of stakeholders is a strength that may improve relevance to practice.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this protocol signals that updated comparative evidence is coming; clinicians should await the final results before changing practice.

item.title: Serum ferritin in children with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD): A systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether serum ferritin concentrations differ between children with ADHD and healthy controls, addressing inconsistent prior findings. It included 21 studies (4,058 ADHD cases and 4,533 controls) and followed PRISMA guidelines.
FINDINGS: The pooled mean difference in serum ferritin between children with ADHD and controls was -9.74 µg/L (95% CI: -16.50 to -2.98). Subgroup analyses showed substantial heterogeneity: larger effects were seen in African studies (-19.28), post-2016 publications (-19.43), smaller studies (<199 participants; -12.12), and studies using DSM-IV-TR criteria (-16.56). Heterogeneity (I²) was high across subgroups.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests lower ferritin in ADHD, but the pooled effect is modest and highly heterogeneous across regions, time periods, and study designs. The wide confidence intervals and inconsistent subgroup patterns limit certainty. The review did not assess risk of bias or adjust for confounders (e.g., diet, comorbidities), and publication bias was not formally excluded. The clinical significance of a ~10 µg/L difference is unclear without data linking ferritin to functional outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify routine ferritin screening or iron supplementation in ADHD solely based on ferritin levels. Future longitudinal studies with standardized ferritin assays and clinical endpoints are needed before considering changes to practice.

item.title: Effects of Benzodiazepines on Heart Failure Outcomes and Adverse Events: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether benzodiazepine (BZD) use for insomnia is associated with adverse heart failure (HF) outcomes in high-risk populations. Eleven observational studies were included, with follow-up ranging from 180 days to 15 years.
FINDINGS: Benzodiazepine use was associated with increased risks of HF incidence (HR = 1.41, 95% CI 1.16–1.72) and HF hospitalization (HR = 1.29, 95% CI 1.01–1.65) compared to non-use. It also showed higher HF hospitalization risk than antipsychotics, z-drugs, and suvorexant. All included studies were observational, limiting causal inference.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests an association between BZD use and worse HF outcomes, but causality cannot be established due to the observational design. Confounding by indication (e.g., insomnia itself may worsen HF outcomes) and lack of randomized data weaken conclusions. The effect sizes are modest and may not translate to clinically meaningful differences in all patients.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Caution is warranted when prescribing BZDs to patients with or at risk of HF, but insomnia management should not be withheld without considering alternatives. Further research—particularly randomized or well-controlled studies—is needed to clarify causality and guide safer prescribing.

item.title: Efficacy of a Prescription-Based Mobile Digital Therapeutic as an Adjunct to Pharmacotherapy for the Acute Phase of Panic Disorder: Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multicenter, single-blind RCT (n=61 completers) tested whether adding a prescription-based mobile digital therapeutic (DTx) to pharmacotherapy improves acute-phase panic disorder symptoms (frequent panic attacks) over 8 weeks. The DTx combined structured CBT modules, just-in-time panic coping, and daily tracking.
FINDINGS: The DTx group achieved a 40.29% (SD 26.68%) reduction in PDSS-SR scores versus 17.61% (SD 30.37%) in controls at week 8 (P=.007). Benefits emerged early (week 2: 26.66% vs 11.05%; P=.02). Responder rate (≥40% PDSS-SR reduction) was higher with DTx (53.12% vs 17.24%; P=.007). Adherence averaged 78.12%; no difference between responders/nonresponders.
INTERPRETATION: The trial suggests adjunctive DTx yields statistically significant and clinically detectable improvements in panic severity and related cognitions, with early onset and sustained effects. Strengths include RCT design, objective adherence metrics, and clinically meaningful responder thresholds. Limitations include small sample, single-blind design (assessors unblinded), short 8-week horizon, and lack of long-term follow-up. Funding sources and adverse events were not reported in the abstract.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: DTx could be considered as a practical adjunct to pharmacotherapy for acute-phase panic disorder, particularly where access to CBT is limited. Clinicians should monitor adherence and integrate app-generated data into routine care, while awaiting replication and longer-term outcomes.

item.title: Association between cortisol levels and psychosis in at-risk and diagnosed individuals: protocol for a systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a systematic review examining whether cortisol levels (a marker of HPA-axis dysregulation) are associated with psychosis in at-risk populations and in patients with diagnosed psychotic disorders. The review will include case-control and cohort studies to clarify the temporal and cross-sectional links between cortisol and psychosis.
FINDINGS: The protocol specifies comprehensive searches across five databases plus Google Scholar, inclusion of case-control and cohort designs, and dual risk-of-bias assessment with the Joanna Briggs Institute tool and GRADE. No results are reported yet; the review is ongoing and registered in PROSPERO.
INTERPRETATION: Because this is a protocol, no empirical findings are available. The planned methodology appears rigorous, but the ultimate strength of the evidence will depend on the quality and heterogeneity of the included studies. Until results are published, clinical implications remain uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this protocol does not change practice. Clinicians should await the completed review to see whether cortisol measurement could aid risk stratification or monitoring in psychosis.

item.title: Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR) for ICU-related psychological distress among adult intensive care survivors: a scoping review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Post-intensive care syndrome includes PTSD, anxiety, and depression after adult ICU admission. EMDR is a trauma-focused therapy, but its evidence in ICU survivors is emerging. This scoping review mapped the literature on EMDR for ICU-related psychological distress.
FINDINGS: Seven publications (six independent samples) were included; participants were adults with ICU-related PTSD symptoms, delirium-related disturbances, or COVID-19 distress. EMDR (standard or R-TEP) was associated with reductions in trauma-related distress; improvements in anxiety/depression were less consistent. Qualitative reports noted better integration of ICU experiences. Methodological heterogeneity, small samples, overlapping cohorts, and limited controlled data constrain conclusions.
INTERPRETATION: Confidence in the evidence is low due to design limitations and small, heterogeneous samples. No controlled trials were identified, so effectiveness remains unproven. The signal of benefit is plausible but preliminary; larger RCTs with standardised outcomes and longer follow-up are needed before EMDR can be recommended routinely in ICU survivors.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: EMDR cannot yet be considered an evidence-based treatment for ICU-related psychological distress. Clinicians may consider it cautiously in selected cases, but should prioritise established trauma-focused therapies with stronger evidence bases and monitor outcomes closely.

item.title: Communication strategies in medical imaging departments for autistic patients. A systematic review exploring person-centred care practices.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PROSPERO-registered, PRISMA-guided) synthesised six studies on communication interventions in medical imaging departments to improve accessibility for autistic patients, primarily in MRI and paediatric settings.
FINDINGS: Five of six studies were paediatric; three focused on MRI. Interventions included picture schedules, at-home procedural videos, and iPad social scripts. Qualitative synthesis identified three themes: flexible communication fosters acceptance, optimised communication improves experience and scan completion, and outcomes should balance patient perspectives with quantitative metrics.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small (n=6), heterogeneous, and at high risk of bias; most studies are paediatric and MRI-focused, limiting generalisability to adults or other imaging modalities. The reported improvements in experience and completion rates are plausible but not quantified with effect sizes or confidence intervals, so clinical significance remains uncertain. The review’s strength lies in its structured synthesis and identification of research gaps rather than definitive effect estimates.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings support trialling flexible, multimodal communication strategies in imaging departments for autistic patients, especially children undergoing MRI, while awaiting higher-quality trials that measure both patient-reported and objective outcomes.

item.title: Treatment Trajectories of Methylphenidate versus Risperidone in Preschool ADHD: A 12-Week Retrospective Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study compared 12-week trajectories of symptom change and functional outcomes between methylphenidate and risperidone monotherapies in preschool-aged boys with ADHD in a naturalistic, non-randomized retrospective chart review.
FINDINGS: Thirty-eight drug-naïve boys (52–72 months) completed 12 weeks of monotherapy (methylphenidate n=20, risperidone n=18). Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA showed no significant Time × Group interaction for core ADHD symptoms (CPRS-R:S subscales, p > 0.05), with both groups improving equally and plateauing after week 6. For broader functioning (SDQ), significant Time × Group interactions emerged (p < 0.05): methylphenidate produced earlier global behavioral improvement by week 3, whereas risperidone showed later gains in conduct problems (after week 6) and emotional symptoms (week 12).
INTERPRETATION: The study’s non-randomized, retrospective design and small, male-only sample limit causal inference and generalizability. Blinding and randomization were absent, and baseline differences were not controlled, raising confounding risk. Despite statistically significant SDQ interactions, effect sizes and clinical relevance are unclear without reported magnitudes. The parallel ADHD symptom reduction suggests no superiority for either drug on core symptoms, while functional differences may reflect distinct timelines rather than differential efficacy.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These preliminary findings do not justify choosing one agent over the other for core ADHD symptoms in preschoolers. Clinicians should await RCTs with larger, mixed-gender samples and longer follow-up before altering practice, while noting possible earlier functional gains with methylphenidate.

item.title: A Problem-Solving Therapy With Apple Watch Support for College Students With Alcohol Use Disorder Symptoms: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested a novel, remote problem-solving therapy augmented by an Apple Watch (PST-APPLE) versus education-only control in college students with alcohol use disorder (AUD) symptoms. It aimed to assess feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary effectiveness on alcohol-related outcomes and drinking motives.
FINDINGS: Twenty-six students (mean age 22.5 years) were randomized 1:1. At 3 months, the intervention group showed reductions in AUDIT (mean difference −4.70, 95% CI −8.69 to −0.70) and in DMQR social (−0.85, 95% CI −1.51 to −0.18) and enhancement (−0.75, 95% CI −1.47 to −0.04) drinking motives versus control. Within-group paired t-tests also indicated reductions in AUDIT and RAPI scores post-intervention.
INTERPRETATION: This pilot RCT suggests PST-APPLE is feasible and acceptable, with small-to-moderate baseline-adjusted effects on alcohol misuse and drinking motives. However, the sample is tiny, not powered for efficacy, and lacks blinding of participants and therapists; effect sizes may be overestimated. Long-term outcomes and generalizability to broader student populations remain unknown.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to change practice; PST-APPLE may be promising for digitally literate college students, but larger, adequately powered trials with longer follow-up are needed before recommending adoption.

item.title: Antidepressant maintenance versus active monitoring after depression remission: a decision analysis and framework linking recurrence probability and patient preferences.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This decision-analysis model compared long-term outcomes of antidepressant maintenance therapy versus active monitoring after remission from major depressive disorder (MDD), quantifying the trade-off between reduced depression recurrence and increased antidepressant exposure across patients with varying prior episode histories.
FINDINGS: Over a 5-year horizon, the model estimated that averting one month of depression required 1.5 additional years of antidepressant use in patients with 4–5 prior episodes, 2.8 years with 2–3 episodes, 5.1 years after one moderate-to-severe episode, and 11.8 years after one mild episode. The trade-off ratio increased steeply with fewer prior episodes, reflecting lower baseline recurrence risk.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides a transparent framework linking recurrence probability, treatment burden, and patient preferences, but relies on modeling assumptions rather than empirical data. The wide variation in trade-off ratios highlights the need for individualized risk–benefit assessment. The model’s validity depends on the accuracy of input parameters (e.g., recurrence rates, episode duration) and may not generalize to settings with different treatment practices or patient populations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This model can guide shared decision-making by translating abstract relapse data into concrete trade-offs, helping clinicians and patients weigh maintenance therapy against active monitoring based on episode history and personal values. However, it should be used cautiously until validated in real-world cohorts.

item.title: Addiction management and rehabilitation programs in Saudi Arabia: a scoping review of current practices and opportunities for healthcare technology integration.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review maps current addiction management and rehabilitation programs in Saudi Arabia and explores opportunities for healthcare technology integration, addressing fragmented evidence and evolving service models in a context with strict legal and social controls.
FINDINGS: Nine studies (1995–2024) showed a shift from detoxification-focused care to multidisciplinary rehabilitation with therapeutic communities and aftercare, but long-term retention was poor, relapse and readmission were common, and community-based services were underused. Social factors like unemployment and family conflict consistently impacted outcomes. Healthcare technology use was minimal, with no studies on telehealth, mobile apps, remote monitoring, or AI-supported care. Methodological quality was moderate overall, with only three high-quality studies.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited and heterogeneous, with moderate methodological quality and no high-quality evaluations of digital interventions. While service evolution is evident, persistent gaps in long-term support and community integration undermine effectiveness. The absence of technology-based studies highlights a major research and implementation gap rather than proven ineffectiveness.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice remains largely traditional, with limited integration of digital tools despite potential benefits. Clinicians should be cautious about extrapolating benefits from other settings; more robust, locally relevant research is needed before advocating widespread adoption of healthcare technologies in Saudi addiction care.

item.title: Ketamine Use Disorder and Entrenchment of Delusional Beliefs: A Case Report.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The case report examines a 36-year-old man with ketamine use disorder (KUD) who developed persistent delusional beliefs over 2 years of heavy ketamine use, highlighting the limited evidence on treating KUD and associated psychotic symptoms.
FINDINGS: The patient met DSM-5-TR criteria for KUD with no prior psychiatric diagnoses (other than alcohol use disorder). His delusions were grandiose and hyper-religious, maintained at delusional intensity despite limited functional impact. No quantitative outcomes (e.g., symptom scales) were reported.
INTERPRETATION: This is a single case report with no comparator, making it impossible to infer causality or generalizability. The lack of standardized treatment data underscores the preliminary nature of the evidence. The clinical significance of the delusions remains unclear due to the absence of functional impairment metrics.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The case underscores the need for vigilance regarding psychotic symptoms in chronic ketamine users but does not inform treatment decisions due to its anecdotal nature. Further research is required to guide management of KUD and its psychiatric sequelae.

item.title: From discovery to proof: a Translation Evidence Map for precision psychiatry.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This Personal View proposes a Translation Evidence Map (TEM) to stage claims in precision psychiatry from discovery (Level 0) to post-deployment monitoring (Level 6), aiming to improve individual-patient decisions by quantifying clinically meaningful heterogeneity across biomarkers, data types, and analytical methods.
FINDINGS: The TEM framework evaluates claims based on measurement reliability, generalisable inference, decision value, safe delivery, and proportionality to risk/clinical need/inaction. Examples include inflammatory and circuit-based depression stratification, psychosis relapse monitoring, and suicidality monitoring. The Map does not replace existing frameworks (e.g., GRADE, biomarker qualification) but identifies the highest defensible claim and next evidence steps for compound precision claims.
INTERPRETATION: The TEM provides a structured approach to assess the maturity of precision psychiatry claims, emphasizing transparency in evidence progression and stakeholder roles. However, as a conceptual framework, it lacks empirical validation or quantitative outcomes. Its utility depends on integration with existing regulatory and clinical pathways, and its external validity remains untested in routine care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This framework may guide clinicians in evaluating emerging precision psychiatry tools but does not yet offer actionable clinical recommendations. Clinicians should await validation studies and regulatory approvals before adopting such methods.

item.title: Subacute effects of ketamine on neural correlates of reward processing.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether ketamine, given to healthy volunteers, alters brain reward processing five hours after infusion (subacute phase) using fMRI during a reward task. The question matters because ketamine’s antidepressant effects may involve reward circuitry, but prior work focused mainly on acute effects. This was a single-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study in 28 healthy adults.
FINDINGS: At 5 hours post-infusion, ketamine did not significantly change brain activation during the Monetary Incentive Delay task in either region-of-interest or whole-brain analyses. Plasma ketamine and norketamine levels confirmed expected pharmacokinetics, but neither drug exposure nor subjective effects correlated robustly with neural activation. No effect sizes or p-values are reported in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: The single-blind, crossover design and healthy volunteer sample limit internal validity; blinding may have been compromised by ketamine’s subjective effects. The absence of detectable changes could reflect true lack of subacute reward-circuit modulation or insufficient power to detect small effects. The study cannot address whether effects would appear in patients with depression or anhedonia, where reward circuitry may be more sensitive. Overall, the evidence is preliminary and does not support subacute modulation of reward processing in healthy individuals under these methods.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify changing practice regarding ketamine’s use for reward-related symptoms. Clinicians should note that any antidepressant benefits likely involve mechanisms beyond subacute normalization of reward-task activation in healthy brains.

item.title: Unlocking School Nurses' Capacity for Suicide Risk Screening: Implications for Multitiered System of Supports.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study investigated how school nurses screen students for suicide risk and whether district-level suicide prevention policies influence their screening methods, self-efficacy, and referral rates. It was a national cross-sectional survey (N = 578) examining school nurses' roles in youth suicide prevention.
FINDINGS: School nurses whose roles were explicitly defined in district suicide prevention policies were more likely to use standardized screening questions. Use of standardized screening was indirectly associated with a higher number of referrals to community services, mediated by increased screening self-efficacy.
INTERPRETATION: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference; associations do not prove that policy integration improves screening or referrals. The mediation by self-efficacy suggests a plausible mechanism, but unmeasured confounders (e.g., school resources, nurse training) could influence results. The study highlights a potential policy lever but requires longitudinal or experimental validation to confirm impact.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: If confirmed, integrating school nurses into formal suicide prevention policies could enhance standardized screening and referral practices, but current evidence is preliminary and does not yet mandate practice changes.

item.title: Law Enforcement Officers and Autism Stigma: Changes Associated With Autism Training.
item.description: PURPOSE: Law enforcement officers (LEOs) frequently interact with autistic individuals, often without autism-specific training. Limited training may contribute to stigmatizing attitudes that influence these encounters. This study evaluated changes in LEOs' autism stigma toward autistic individuals following autism training. METHODS: A nonrandomized pre-post intervention design examined changes in autism stigma among 438 LEOs who attended autism training in California or Florida.

item.title: Intrinsic capacity modifies the risk of depression and anxiety through metabolomic signature.
item.description: BACKGROUND: The World Health Organization (WHO) developed an assessment for healthy aging termed intrinsic capacity (IC). However, the association between IC and depression/anxiety remains poorly understood, with limited understanding of the underlying metabolic mechanisms. METHODS: This prospective cohort study comprised 212,033 UK Biobank participants recruited between 2006 and 2010. We calculated a UK Biobank-adapted four-domain IC deficit score using seven functional status indicators across psychological, sensory, vitality, and locomotor domains.
